This is fake news - an increasingly common occurrence from the NYT.

The person was not 'sent to prison by an algorithm.' The program they're talking about is used to determine recidivism, or reoffense, rates of criminals. It's just a tool that can be used to help guide sentencing, probation, etc as it was in the case mentioned - the individual was already tried and convicted and the software played no role there. The arrest rate per capita in the US is around 3/100 though that does likely include people being arrested multiple times. In any case, that's about 3%. By comparison the people this program selects tend to be arrested within 2 years at a rate greater than 60%. That's a bit misleading since I'm comparing the general population to somebody who likely has already been entered into the justice system, but even if you only consider previous offenders - the system performs well.

This article is a spin piece that's rephrasing the recent flurry of articles about 'racist algorithms' in a different way. Those articles were met with a very negative reception. These articles are, fundamentally, trying to claim is that since race is obviously included in these algorithms it's supposed to be racist considering that, for instance, a 'green' individual is vastly more likely to reoffend than any other individual. It may not be fair because it's considering things that the person in question can't change about themselves, but human courts, probation hearings, etc do the exact same thing. And in the case of the humans, their biases are going to be driven by prejudice and even their mood (fun fact - people who see a judge earlier in the day are more likely to receive lenient sentences) rather than raw data. The cold nature of algorithms is disconcerting, but it's simultaneously also their best feature. I would never agree with using them for preemptive action, but for post-facto judgement I think we'll find them to be leagues ahead of humans.

ed Another thing I'd ad is that we're already at the stage where it's becoming impossible for programmers to tell you exactly why an AI system is coming to the conclusion it did. The developers who wrote the Go playing AI who crushed the world's strongest human could give you broad strokes about the things it was considering, but how it precisely weighted and applied these on a per move basis was far outside their comprehension. Ultimately what matters is does the algorithm function as a 'black box'? If you ask a computer what 15 + 18 is you don't care how it comes to its conclusion, so long as it tells you 33 and also tells you similarly accurate answers for all other similar problems. As we advance technologically algorithms are going to be able to answer vastly more complex questions. How it gets to the solution is going to be increasingly out of reach.
